title: sensor-registry-stall.json's first non-empty result since its 2026-09-07 promotion: memoryhole/readings is two nights behind, and the code shows why a run that does not finish writes nothing at all rather than a partial, disclosed reading
statement:
autonomy/log.jsonl carries six committed registry-stall-check entries, one per night since the sensor's 2026-09-07 promotion (2026-09-08 through 2026-09-13). The first five all read {"checked": [...four registers...], "stale": []}. Tonight's, 2026-09-13T05:49:09+00:00, is the first to carry a non-empty stale list: {"days_behind": 2, "newest_committed_date": "2026-09-10", "register": "memoryhole/readings"}. memoryhole/readings/ (and memoryhole/snapshots/) confirm this directly: the newest committed file in each is dated 2026-09-10, with no 2026-09-11 or 2026-09-12 file of any kind -- not even a partial one. autonomy/log.jsonl's own step=="memoryhole-run" entries (27 total, one per successfully completed night since the workflow's first run on 2026-08-15) end at 2026-09-11T09:36:33+00:00, recording the reading of 2026-09-10; no memoryhole-run entry exists for 2026-09-12 or 2026-09-13. The other three registers the sensor watches did not stall over the same span: foreknown/snapshots and foreknown/reaction/snapshots both advanced on schedule (autonomy/log.jsonl foreknown-notary-run, 2026-09-12T09:34:22+00:00, date 2026-09-12) and darkocean/snapshots likewise (darkocean-run and darkocean-continuity, both 2026-09-12T08:5x:xx+00:00, date 2026-09-11) -- the stall is specific to memoryhole, not a broader outage, the same way obs-2026-09-06-1.json's export.py crash was shown specific to the foreknown-side registers by the same method (comparing which registers kept advancing over the identical span).

practice/src/practice/memoryhole/run.py's run() explains why a memoryhole stall leaves no partial trace where a foreknown stall at least sometimes might: every institution's discovery query and every sampled page's history/snapshot fetch happens in a single Python-level loop held entirely in memory (institutions/pages/entries lists, lines 316-345 before this run's edit), and the reading is written exactly once, at the very end (write_json(reading_path, reading), formerly line 354), with the autonomy.append call immediately after it. Nothing before that point touches memoryhole/readings/, memoryhole/snapshots/ manifests, or autonomy/log.jsonl. .github/workflows/memoryhole.yml's own comment already names the reason a run can run long: the CDX server is 'slow and unreliable' with a measured '19% 504 rate under concurrency', which is why the workflow budgets a 240-minute timeout-minutes ceiling on the 'Reading of the completed UTC day' step specifically -- a ceiling that, before tonight's fix, could only ever produce two outcomes: the run finishes inside 240 minutes and everything is written, or GitHub kills it and literally nothing is. Because main()'s --date always defaults to 'yesterday' computed at the moment a later run actually executes, a night lost this way is not retried by any subsequent run -- the next scheduled run always targets a newly-computed 'yesterday', permanently skipping the missed date. This is not the first time this exact failure shape has cost memoryhole a night: practice/tests/test_fetch.py's own docstring records that 'the memoryhole run of 2026-08-26 died an hour into the reading of 2026-08-25 with http.client.RemoteDisconnected and committed nothing', fixed by widening fetch.py's retry ladder to catch connection-boundary exceptions that previously escaped every 'except SourceUnavailable' in run.py -- a different specific cause of the identical outward symptom (a memoryhole night committed nothing at all), the same relationship the four foreknown/darkocean-side causes in staleness.py's own module docstring bear to each other.

Repaired tonight: memoryhole/run.py now tracks a wall-clock deadline (MAX_RUN_SECONDS = 200*60, an injectable clock defaulting to time.monotonic) across both the institutions loop and the per-page loop. Once the deadline passes, remaining institutions are recorded with source: null and skipped: "over_time_budget" (excluded from verify.py's check_memoryhole sample-reconciliation the same way any institution with no preserved discovery source already is), and remaining pages are recorded as class "unverifiable", reason "over_time_budget", with no history fetched -- the same visible-rather-than-silently-dropped shape the existing MAX_CHANGED_PAGES/over_nightly_fetch_cap already uses for its own budget. A new top-level time_budget block ({max_seconds, institutions_skipped, pages_skipped}) is written into every reading, and the same two counts are folded into the autonomy.append detail (over_time_budget). This converts a run killed by the workflow's outer 240-minute timeout from committing nothing into self-truncating well inside that ceiling and committing a real, visibly-partial reading -- but it does not and cannot recover the already-lost 2026-09-11 reading, which this design still has no mechanism to backfill.
method: Read every autonomy/log.jsonl entry with step=="registry-stall-check" (six, one per night since 2026-09-07) and step=="memoryhole-run" (27, spanning 2026-08-15 through 2026-09-11) to find the first stale result and the last successful reading. Listed memoryhole/readings/ and memoryhole/snapshots/ directly to confirm the newest committed date in each independently of the log. Cross-checked autonomy/log.jsonl for foreknown-notary-run, darkocean-run and darkocean-continuity entries dated 2026-09-12 to confirm the other three watched registers did not stall over the same span. Read practice/src/practice/memoryhole/run.py in full (the institutions loop, the pages loop, read_page, and the single write_json/autonomy.append call at the end) and .github/workflows/memoryhole.yml (the 240-minute timeout-minutes on the reading step, and its own comment about CDX server unreliability) to trace why an unfinished run commits nothing. Read practice/tests/test_fetch.py's module docstring and practice/src/practice/fetch.py's Client.fetch exception handling for the precedent of an earlier memoryhole night (2026-08-25) lost the same way to a different specific cause, already fixed. Implemented and tested the time-budget change (practice/src/practice/memoryhole/run.py; practice/tests/test_memoryhole_run.py, two new tests: an ample-budget run skips nothing, a zero-budget run still writes a complete, verify.py-clean reading with every institution and page marked over_time_budget). Ran the full suite (python -m pytest practice/tests) and python -m pip install -e ./practice beforehand; both green.

figures.prior_full_night_loss_precedent: 2026-08-25 (RemoteDisconnected, fixed in fetch.py, documented in test_fetch.py)

worth_watching_because: This is the mechanism sensor-registry-stall.json was promoted to catch, firing for the first time under real conditions rather than a reconstructed pre-repair tree: a register two nights behind, with autonomy/log.jsonl's own trace of the underlying job simply absent rather than showing a recorded failure. The proposal's own module docstring (practice/src/practice/staleness.py) names four mechanically distinct prior causes of this identical outward symptom and observes that none of the four has ever been seen to self-correct on its own; tonight's memoryhole gap is a fifth, and -- like 2026-08-25's RemoteDisconnected loss before it -- has the same shape: a slow, flaky external archive, a job that holds an entire night's work in memory, and a single all-or-nothing write at the end. Unlike the four foreknown/darkocean-side causes, this one is structural rather than a one-time logic bug: nothing about memoryhole/run.py changed between the five clean nights and this one, and nothing rules out the same shape of loss recurring on any future night the archive is slow enough, for as long as the function has no internal ceiling of its own tighter than the workflow's external one. That is what tonight's repair addresses -- not a specific bug in what happened this time (the record does not show, and does not need to show, why the run ran long; only that the code guaranteed a long run would cost the whole night rather than most of it), but the general shape shared with the 2026-08-25 precedent.
left_alone: Not attempting to backfill the lost 2026-09-11 or 2026-09-12 readings by invoking memoryhole.run with an explicit --date from inside this pass: doing so could itself run for hours against the same slow archive this observation is about, inside a session budgeted for discovery rather than a multi-hour nightly job, and could race the next scheduled memoryhole workflow run over the same commit path. That gap stays a permanent, disclosed hole in the record, the same way obs-2026-08-27-1's confirmed foreknown-notary gap and the four-nights-missing discovery-pass gap (obs-2026-09-11-1.json) each stayed holes rather than being reconstructed after the fact -- this observatory does not backfill a silence into a false continuity. Not adding automatic backfill logic to memoryhole.yml or run.py's main() (e.g. detecting and re-reading a skipped prior date): that would change the workflow's operational semantics beyond tonight's narrower fix, and deciding whether missed nights should ever be retried automatically, versus staying a visible permanent gap by design (the same choice this observatory has made everywhere else so far), is the maintainer's call. Not lowering MAX_RUN_SECONDS further or otherwise trying to make the archive itself faster -- the number is set with margin under the workflow's existing 240-minute ceiling, not tuned against any measurement of how long a healthy night actually takes, since only one over-budget night exists so far to measure against. Checked and left unchanged: sensor-resolution-reappearance-coverage.json (gdacs-tc-1001305 still OPEN, no second closure since 2026-08-28); sensor-source-reconfirmation-blind-spot.json (gdacs-fl-1103815's datemodified still frozen at 2026-09-03T13:36:40 -- confirmed directly against foreknown/snapshots/2026-09-12/gdacs.json, one more frozen night added to the run obs-2026-09-12-1.json already tracked -- no new instance to add). No memoryhole verdicts: the newest reading remains memoryhole/readings/2026-09-10.json (already reviewed by obs-2026-09-11-1.json and obs-2026-09-12-1.json with zero rule-layer abstentions across 31 entries); no new reading exists tonight to review, which this observation's own subject already explains.
